# Pixel-Perfect Render Pipeline & Camera

> Authoring guidance: .claude/docs/templates/guidance/game-design-document-guide.md (load per-section as you author — do not read entirely).

> **Status**: Designed
> **Author**: user + systems-designer, engine-programmer, gameplay-programmer, game-designer, ux-designer, creative-director, qa-lead (via /design-system, autonomous)
> **Last Updated**: 2026-10-28 (second delegated rulings; see Amendments) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* *(Amended 2026-10-27 — user rulings)* *(Amended 2026-10-28 — delegated rulings)*
> **Last Verified**: 2026-10-25
> **Creative Director Review (CD-GDD-ALIGN)**: APPROVED 2026-10-26 (after one CONCERNS round: header de-over-claimed, jolt triggers unified, stale values rewritten in place; user decisions 2026-10-26: zoom ladder in both directions supersedes single-step-out; expand ratified; calibration guide-only)
> **Amendments after sign-off**: 2026-10-26 — /consistency-check: Player Controller values landed (120 / 180 px/s) and every derived number re-run; zoom-ladder rewrite completed in place (States `ZOOMED`, D.5 `zoom_ladder`); C7 extension — all solver length knobs scale by `s = field_h / 360` (orchestrator decision, systems-designer finding; τ_follow safe range now 0–0.20 s, L_MAX 48–75 px). 56 passages marked *consistency check*. No re-review of CD-GDD-ALIGN was run.
> **Amendments after the first design review (2026-10-27)**: four BLOCKING findings and the RECOMMENDED set were applied in place and every touched paragraph or row is marked *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*: (1) the look-ahead / mouse-aim loop is opened by definition (C4, C11, D.7, D.14b); (2) every pose term settles per axis so a still scene's pose is constant (D.6, D.7, SETTLE_EPS); (3) the "identical at 60 and 144 fps" contract is replaced by a stated bound, with the lag measured after the update (C3, D.6); (4) the Y-sort tie-break is a class rank plus a stable entity ID, never `x` or creation order, with a rule for passable doors (PR-5, D.12). The RECOMMENDED set also changed: `τ_follow_eff = τ_follow × min(1, s)` with a zoom-step state transition; even logical fields; a world-anchored z-band fallback; a solver-written camera transform; BODY_TRANSFER rebase and an L = 0 wake; solver guards; draw-call caps per field; an analytic flash governor; picture-relative `world_to_hud`; PR-15 additions; and a rebuilt Dependencies table. No CD-GDD-ALIGN re-review was run.
> **Amendments after the re-review (2026-10-27, delegated best-judgment rulings)**: two BLOCKING findings were fixed and the RECOMMENDED set applied in place; every touched paragraph or row is marked *(Amended 2026-10-27 — re-review)*, with *delegated ruling R4* where a ruling applies. (1) **Mouse aim (R4)**: the Player Controller's form is canonical — D.14b publishes `f_q = floor(f/Q)·Q` and `cursor_world_aim = f_q + cursor_off`, the Controller subtracts the fixed `AIM_ORIGIN`, the chest-based subtraction is gone from D.14b / D.7, `cursor_px` is physical window px (the engine-reference does not settle the unit of `get_mouse_position()` under stretch: [UNV], an in-engine AC gates it); the creative-director's avatar-anchored `p` was not adopted and its cost is stated. (2) **Flash predicate (D.15)**: `Y_ref` is a running extremum with direction tracking, with smooth-sine fixtures. (3) Added **D.6b** (offset-quantised follow, default candidate) and **D.8b** (limits clamp order); corrected the inner-box jump direction, the zoom examples, the low-fps lag bound and the safe-range inequality; settle is `max(t_settle_f, t_settle_L)`; run weighting keyed on `loco_state` and octant; `D.12` namespace-tagged `entity_id`; `D.13` union-rect bands; D5 withholding as a static `ZOOM_MIN_K` table with the predicted-withheld table; engine-facing rules (effective-value project-key tests, named render hook, wiring (iii), paused-resize `UPDATE_ONCE`, reading-face rasterisation, debanding); dual-path Camera2D assertions and host-driven parallax; testability rewrites and a Test fixtures paragraph; five dependency rows. **X14 closed 2026-10-28 (delegated ruling R12: reference machines RM-DESKTOP and RM-DECK named); D79 and D5 are "default applied, confirmed 2026-10-28 (delegated ruling R20)".** CD-GDD-ALIGN has not been re-run (Open Question 28).
> **Amendments after the user rulings (2026-10-27)**: the user ruled on the design-review decisions ("I agree with all of your recommendations on those decisions"; "yes to all" on the held list). Applied here, each touched paragraph or row marked *(Amended 2026-10-27 — user rulings)*: (1) **flash counting unit** `F = ceil(n_transitions / 2)` ratified and `FLASH_MAX_PER_S` area-weighted with the creative-director exemptions (PR-13 g, D.15; X9 / D91, user ruling); (2) **reduce flashing defaults ON at first launch** (PR-13 c, PR-14, UI Requirements 2; X10 / D79, default applied, confirmed 2026-10-28 (delegated ruling R20)); (3) **look-ahead weighted toward movement while running** (C4, D.7, `LOOKAHEAD_RUN_WEIGHT`; D6 option B, user ruling); (4) **mouse-aim origin** read as Player Controller's fixed reference chest `AIM_ORIGIN` (D.14b; D10, user ruling); (5) **a zoom step that fails its caps is withheld, never bought back by cutting content** (D.16, Open Question 21; D5, default applied, confirmed 2026-10-28 (delegated ruling R20)). X14 (reference machine) was open here and is closed by delegated ruling R12 (Open Question 20). No CD-GDD-ALIGN re-review was run.
> **Amendments after the second delegated rulings (2026-10-28)**: (1) **blockers recomputed from the formulas (G4)**: the D.3 residual prose and the `expand` AC now include the cap-bound residual (3840×1080 gives 480/480); the PR-11 / D.17 / Game Feel "never twice in a frame" promise is scoped to f_render ≥ 60 and the frame-step AC is rewritten per rate (40 fps alternates +1/+2); the D.15 `Y_scale` row states the floor's purpose and the photosensitivity fixtures are recomputed (formula unchanged); (2) **R12**: RM-DESKTOP and RM-DECK and the release-export measurement build replace every "reference hardware not named" passage, performance criteria are "pending spike" on those machines, Open Question 20 is closed; (3) **R20 / R21**: no open user-decision or pending-confirmation item remains (Open Questions 16, 21, 25 decided). *(Amended 2026-10-28 — delegated rulings G4, R12, R20, R21)*
> **Amendments after the cross-GDD fix pass (2026-10-28)**: every touched paragraph or row is marked *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix)*. (1) **Sort `entity_id`**: the kernel allocates no IDs (kernel CR-8); Body's `actor_id` is block-local (BDY-20), so every class, actors and horrors included, uses the publisher's namespace-tagged ID registered with this GDD (PR-5, D.12). (2) **Aim shift `S` (G4 recompute)**: D.14b defines `S = f_q.x − floor(pos_curr.x)` with its oracle and fixtures (60/90/144 fps); the 32.4 px figure is the dt→0 upper bound of the lag, not a value at any shipped rate; the Example, Edge Case, Open Question 18 and the acceptance criterion now quote `S` and `|ΔS| ≤ 36 px`. (3) **Settle time for exact oracles (G3/G4)**: D.6 names `t_exact = 10·τ_eff` = 1.8 s (the unsettled lag is 0.0014 px) next to `t_95`, and every floor-exact or count oracle that started at `3·τ_eff` (the D.14b `S` AC, the D.6b offset ACs, the D.6b offset-change count, C3 step 12 and Open Question 12) now starts at `t_exact`; `t_95` stays a 95 % claim. *(Amended 2026-10-28 — cross-GDD fix; G4 recompute)*
> **Implements Pillar**: The World Never Lies (P1 — no mask, vignette, fog or full-frame gamma between a lit pixel and the screen); Dread Before Chaos and Sanity Rewrites Reality (P2/P4 — no uncaused pixel motion, so tremor and glide stay readable and the frame is an anchor the Filter cannot move); The Web Watches (P3 — the camera never reads world state, and the web's drift stays readable on a grid that does not crawl)

## Summary

The Pixel-Perfect Render Pipeline & Camera is the surface every visual system draws onto and the window the player sees through: a 640×360 logical world scaled by a whole number to the display, rendered with nearest sampling and pixel snapping so no pixel ever moves without a cause in the world; a HUD on its own layer that world light, the sanity filter and camera motion can never touch; a draw-order contract that makes a 3/4-oblique ship read correctly; and a camera that is a window, not a sensor — it follows the player and leans where their beam points, responds to nothing the world does, holds still when the ship does, and cuts rather than pans. It exists because the art bible's identity (*What You Light, You Can Read*) and three pillars rest on an image that is faithful to the simulation at the scale of one art pixel, and because the lighting-budget spike that decides the renderer's cost cannot run without the pipeline it measures.

> **Quick reference** — Layer: `Foundation` · Priority: `MVP` · Key deps: `None` upstream (contracts: Command & Simulation Layer CR-10/11; art bible 8.1–8.4, 7.0); 17 downstream dependents *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*

## Overview

The Pixel-Perfect Render Pipeline & Camera is the surface every visual system of The Synaptic Sea draws onto, and the window through which the player sees it. It fixes a **logical resolution of 640×360** scaled by an integer to the player's display (3× at 1080p, 4× at 1440p, 6× at 2160p, 2× on a Steam Deck), renders the world into its own viewport with nearest-neighbour sampling and pixel snapping so that every art pixel is a crisp square of screen pixels, keeps the HUD on a separate root-viewport layer that the world's glow, ambient and occlusion can never touch, and owns the **camera**: what it follows, how it moves, where it may not go, and the integer zoom steps it may take. It also owns the draw-order contract that makes a 3/4-oblique ship read correctly — floors never sort, wall faces and actors sort together by Y, caps draw above actors — and the single full-screen hook point where the Perception Filter is allowed to corrupt what a low-sanity player sees, below the HUD and never touching it.

The player never interacts with this system directly. They experience it as an image that is faithful: the one-pixel wander of a lying needle and the two-pixel identity bands on a crewmate's helmet stay legible because nothing ever shimmers or blurs; the edge of their own light is drawn as Lighting computes it, never softened or extended by a mask; the frame holds still when the ship does, and moves only as the simulation moves.

It exists because the art bible's whole identity rests on it: *What You Light, You Can Read* needs true 2D occlusion (not a vignette), legibility at one art pixel, and a HUD exempt from world light (art bible Principle 1, 7.0, 8.1–8.4), and the lighting-budget spike that decides the renderer's cost (8.12) cannot run without the pipeline it measures. Seventeen systems, across sixteen rows of the Interactions table (Settings & Input Rebinding and Accessibility Settings share one row — see Dependencies), rest on it directly, and every presentation system inherits its contract *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*: subscribe to the kernel as `PRESENTATION`, read last-committed state, interpolate with `tick_alpha`, write only what is drawn (Command & Simulation Layer CR-10, CR-11). Without it, the game would still simulate correctly and look wrong — which, for a game whose pillar is *The World Never Lies*, is the same as being wrong.

**Design-level only.** `SubViewport` vs root rendering, stretch and snap settings, whether lights render at base or native resolution (the spike's pass A/B), `Camera2D` smoothing vs manual interpolation — these are implementation choices → **becomes an ADR** (render pipeline / tick-source ADRs). *(Framing: technical infrastructure, no ADR yet to cite, fantasy felt indirectly — the recommended options for a `Core`/`Foundation` system under `autonomous` automation.)*

## Player Fantasy

*Indirect — the player never meets this system; they meet a stillness it keeps.*

**When the ship is still, the screen is still.** The game teaches the player to read motion as evidence. A needle that shakes a pixel is a stressed hull warning them. A needle that glides slowly with nothing in the ship to explain it is lying. The four trim bands on a crewmate's helmet are who that is. All of this lives at the scale of one or two art pixels, so it only works if no pixel ever moves for a reason that isn't in the world: no shimmer from a non-integer scale, no camera crawl from rounding, no actor jittering a pixel against the floor as the camera follows. Every pixel that changes was changed by something in the world.

The anchor moment is on the first sortie. The player stands in a dead scrubber bay with their beam on a wall gauge. They stop walking and the frame stops with them. Then the needle moves. Because nothing else on screen moved, the player knows the motion belongs to the ship, or to their own mind, and not to the screen. They lean in to see whether it shakes or glides, and that judgement is the game. The comfort is structural: *if I saw it move, something moved it.*

**Pillars served.** *Dread Before Chaos*: "Every breach is preceded by a tell a careful player could have perceived (sound, light, gauge drift, hull stress)" — gauge drift is perceivable only if render noise can neither fake it nor hide it. *Sanity Rewrites Reality*: "the lie extends from the gauge to the sprite" — the art bible's settle/tremor/glide grammar (7.3) is how a player tells the lie from the warning, and a pipeline that adds its own motion corrupts both. *The World Never Lies*: the rendering stack is neither instrument nor perception, so it may not be wrong either. *The Web Watches*: filament movement at ≤ 1 art px/s (art bible 2.11) is readable only on a grid that does not crawl.

**Design tests.**
- If we are debating a presentation effect that moves world pixels with no cause in the world (sub-pixel smoothing, eased camera lag that overshoots, non-integer zoom, a softening filter, screen shake) against holding the grid: hold the grid, or move the effect into the world (a needle, a sprite, a light).
- The fantasy has failed if a player can see a one-art-pixel movement that no system put there. Two cases count: a static scene, and a followed actor that shifts relative to the floor while the camera tracks it. That is a counterfeit tremor or a counterfeit glide — a Pillar 2 and Pillar 4 violation, not a cosmetic bug. It is testable on day one with a frame-diff: hold the sim with no committed change and the camera target still, and the only world pixels allowed to differ between frames are those owned by a declared animating source (flicker, scrolling medium, web drift); then walk an actor across a static room, and the actor-to-floor offset may change only by whole art pixels in step with committed position.

*What this section does not claim.* The pipeline does not make the world honest; the kernel does. It does not make motion meaningful; the art bible's grammar does. It does not make a reading true; the HUD frame stays put and undimmed (HR-1), but the needle inside it may lie under class (b). It does not own the edge of the light — Lighting and Principle 1 do; the pipeline's part is only that no mask, vignette, fog layer or edge-darkening ever sits between a lit world pixel and the screen, which is a prohibition in Core Rules, not a fantasy. The image is up to one tick behind committed state and never ahead of it (kernel `tick_alpha` clamps at 1). Under lighting pass A the cone edge is a 3-px stair-step at 1080p, and this section does not promise a smooth one. *(Alternatives considered: "the edge belongs to the light" — evocative but credits the pipeline with Lighting's guarantee; "a porthole, not a lens" — accurate camera policy, but policy is not a moment the player feels.)*

**Downstream implications carried into Section C and Game Feel.** Any whole-frame shake counterfeits a tremor, the honest Tell of 2.7: hull stress goes into real needles, dust direction and sprites, not into the frame, and whether any shake survives (e.g. breach impact after the tell has landed) is decided explicitly against design test 1. The commonest way this fantasy fails is the followed actor and the world rounding to different integers in the same frame, so QA tests motion during follow, not only a still scene. The HUD exemption is anchoring, not truth.

## Detailed Design

### Core Rules

*Specialists consulted: systems-designer (primary), engine-programmer, gameplay-programmer, game-designer, ux-designer. Disagreements resolved and logged 2026-10-26; items the specialists could not resolve are in Open Questions.*


**Vocabulary.** *Base px* (*art px*): one pixel of the 640×360 logical grid. *Screen px*: one pixel of the window. *k*: the world's integer scale (screen px per base px). *k_base*: the effective base scale — the manual `k` when Settings sets one below Auto, else the automatic `k` (C6, D.5) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. *H*: the HUD's integer scale, independent of k. *Picture*: the region of the window that shows the game (the window unless letterboxed). *World viewport*: the `SubViewport` holding every lit thing; its canvas **is the current body's frame** (PR-6 C2). *Body*: a Ship Body & Interior Physics object with its own reference frame (home-ship, derelict, pod, detached section). *Sort origin*: the base-px row an object sorts by on the Y-sorted layer. *Pose*: the camera's output — integer base-px position in the body frame plus the current k. *`present_time`*: the pipeline's render-rate clock (PR-9). *Tick*, *`tick_alpha`*, *read view*, *`PRESENTATION`*: as the kernel GDD defines them (CR-10, CR-11, D.3).

---

**PR-1. Logical resolution and integer scale.** The world is authored at **640×360 base px** (registry: `BASE_RESOLUTION`) (art bible 8.1, decided) and drawn at an integer scale `k = floor(min(W / 640, H / 360))` where `W × H` is the window's **pixel** size — never derived from DPI; `content_scale_factor` stays 1.0 and `allow_hidpi` behaviour on the Deck and on Windows ≥ 125 % scaling is logged by spike step 11 (→ D for the variable table). The **minimum window is 1280×720** (registry: `MIN_WINDOW`) (C-R; `Window.min_size` `[BIN]`), so `k ≥ 2` on every display. Nothing in the world is ever drawn at a non-integer scale; the only non-integer text anywhere is the vector reading face on the chart-table layer (7.1). At every window size the player sees square, unblurred base pixels; the trade is the picture size, never pixel integrity. The player may choose k below the automatic value in Settings ("integer world scale: Auto + list", PR-14) — see PR-2 for why a manual k forces `keep`.

| Window (screen px) | k | `keep`: picture and bars | `expand`: logical size (base px) | Tiles in view (expand) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1280×720 | 2 | 1280×720, none | 640×360 | 13.3 × 7.5 |
| **1280×800 (Steam Deck)** | 2 | 1280×720, 40 top + 40 bottom | 640×400 | 13.3 × 8.3 |
| 1366×768 | 2 | 1280×720, 43/43 L/R, 24/24 T/B | 682×384 (even; 1/1 residual) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* | 14.2 × 8.0 |
| 1365×768 (odd width) | 2 | 1280×720, 42/43 L/R, 24/24 T/B | 682×384 (the logical size is always even, so the engine never sees an odd or fractional base; the 1 px residual is letterboxed, 0/1 — what the engine draws in it is step 11's) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* | 14.2 × 8.0 |
| 1600×900 | 2 | 1280×720, 160/160 L/R, 90/90 T/B (36 % of the screen black) | 800×450 | 16.7 × 9.4 |
| **1920×1080** | 3 | none | 640×360 | 13.3 × 7.5 |
| 1920×1200 | 3 | 1920×1080, 60/60 T/B | 640×400 | 13.3 × 8.3 |
| **2560×1440** | 4 | none | 640×360 | 13.3 × 7.5 |
| 2560×1080 (21:9) | 3 | 1920×1080, 320/320 L/R | 852×360 (even; 2/2 residual) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* | 17.8 × 7.5 |
| **3440×1440 (ultrawide)** | 4 | 2560×1440, 440/440 L/R | 860×360 | 17.9 × 7.5 |
| **3840×2160** | 6 | none | 640×360 | 13.3 × 7.5 |

*Rationale.* 640×360 is the only common base that lands on an integer at 720p, 1080p, 1440p and 2160p (8.1's table), so the four sizes the bible calls common need no policy at all; PR-2 exists for everything else. *Alternative rejected:* fractional scaling with a sharpening filter — it breaks 8.0's single grid and makes the 1 px contour, the 2 px bands and the 2 px fringe uneven widths, which 5.6's minimum-feature rule forbids. *Engine fact that makes this rule load-bearing:* `project.godot` today has no `[display]` block and no `rendering/textures` or `rendering/2d/snap` keys, so the project currently runs at the engine built-ins — 1152×648, stretch `disabled`, `fractional`, LINEAR-filtered, unsnapped `[BIN]` — and looks "almost right" in the editor at 1×. PR-15 is the guard.

---

**PR-2. Aspect: `keep` for the spike, `expand` as the IDEAL, both bounded; bars are true black.**

- **`keep` (letterbox).** The picture is `640k × 360k`, centred; the remainder is bars. This is the spike architecture (8.4) and the **default until 8.12 step 2 and step 11 have run**, because the world viewport is a fixed 640×360 and nothing resizes.
- **`expand` (IDEAL, 8.1/8.10, post-spike).** The world viewport's logical size becomes `(2·floor(W/(2k)), 2·floor(H/(2k)))` (always even; D.3), clamped to **≤ 960×540** at default zoom (PROVISIONAL cap = 1.5× base; → D), remainder letterboxed; the base size and k both stay integer at every window (C-R); the **HUD rect is pinned to the `k_base` picture rect** (never the window, never the zoomed picture), so the HUD does not move on a zoom step even when a ladder field leaves a few black pixels inside it (D.5) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. The camera stays centred on the same target, so an ultrawide player sees more void left and right and a Deck player 20 more rows above and below.
- **Manual k forces `keep`.** A player-chosen k below the automatic value under `expand` would be a permanently wider frame (at 1080p, k = 2 gives 960×540 — exactly the zoom-out view, as the default), which the game-designer's decision forbids ("never a wider default frame"; the frame is changed only by the player's `zoom_in` / `zoom_out` steps, PR-6 C6 *(Amended 2026-10-26 — consistency check)*). So when `k < k_auto`, aspect is `keep` regardless of the setting. *(Systems-designer resolution of a conflict between the Settings list and the camera decision — flagged for the ux-designer and game-designer to confirm.)*

*The honesty caveat on "more void, not more information" (8.1).* The claim holds in the dark states (2.4–2.8), where everything outside the beam is black whichever width the frame is. It does **not** fully hold in two cases: (i) at 3440×1440 under `expand` the half-width is ≈ 9 tiles, so the narrow cone's 8-tile reach (8.3) fits entirely on screen where a 16:9 player's is clipped at 6.7 tiles; (ii) in the home-ship stable state (2.3) every fixture is on and a wider frame shows more lit ship. A 1600×900 player under `expand` sees 25 % more in each axis than a 1080p player. The cap bounds the gap; it does not remove it. **Routed to creative-director** with the recommendation to accept `expand` (a third of the screen black at 1600×900 is a worse experience than a slightly wider frame in a co-op horror game with no competitive stake) and to record the gap in Edge Cases. Second cost: under pass B (PR-7) light is paid per lit screen pixel — 4.95 M px at 3440×1440 against 2.07 M at 1080p; under pass A the cost grows only to 860×360 base px. The spike measures pass B at 1080p only; `expand` under pass B is a post-spike measurement.

*Bars.* Letterbox bars are **true black, outside the world `SubViewport`**, untouched by the Perception Filter pass and by any camera jolt (C-R). Because the void inside the world is also near-black (0–1 % ambient, 2.5), a bar could be mistaken for unlit hull: the ux-designer recommends a **1-HUD-px Graphite hairline at the picture edge** — routed to art-director (it is a UI mark, 4.6 palette). What the engine actually draws in the remainder under `keep` is NOT SOURCEABLE (step 11).

*Deck safe area (PROVISIONAL).* The HUD is authored **anchor-relative to the visible picture rect**, never the window, with the 7.0 safe margin of 5 % of the picture rounded up to whole HUD px per axis (registry `safe_margin`, the HUD & Suit Layer's formula): 32 × 18 HUD px at 1920×1080, H 3; 22 × 14 HUD px at 1280×800, H 3 *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from hud-and-suit-layer)* — and must survive a fractional HUD canvas (the picture divided by H is not always integer) and both aspects (C-R). The Deck has no notch; the margin is ergonomic and the ux-designer may raise it per device. Deck *text* size is PR-12's problem.

*Fullscreen.* Default `MODE_FULLSCREEN` (borderless window covering the screen, `Window.mode = 3` `[BIN]`) rather than `EXCLUSIVE_FULLSCREEN` for Alt-Tab safety `[UNV]`; any mode or size change fires `Viewport.size_changed` `[BIN]` and is handled as one `RESCALING` frame (C.2) by **one pipeline-root node that is the only writer** of `SubViewport.size`, `size_2d_override` and the camera limits rect (consumed by the solver, C8), and the only caller of `HudLayout` (the HUD & Suit Layer's layout function, which computes the HUD anchors) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from hud-and-suit-layer)* (→ ADR, with PR-7's wiring).

---

**PR-3. The layer model.** One root viewport, one world viewport, and `CanvasLayer`s above it. The question that assigns a thing to a layer is 7.0's: *who produced the information?* — the ship goes in the world and must be lit to read; the suit and the chart table are screen-space and never lit. **The HUD is in a different viewport, not merely a different layer** (engine-programmer): world lights, glow, `CanvasModulate`, the Filter pass on the container and the camera transform cannot reach it by construction, so HR-1, HR-6 and HR-13 are promised structurally. The trade-off is that nothing that must *mix* (a diegetic element lit by the world) may live there — it goes in the world.

| # | Layer (bottom → top) | Where | Scaled by | Lit / glow / ambient / occlusion | Perception Filter | Camera jolt | Contents |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | **World** | `SubViewport` inside a `SubViewportContainer` | k | **yes** — the only layer that is (`use_hdr_2d`, `use_debanding`, filter, snap set on this viewport's own members `[BIN]`; never on the root, which stays SDR-exact for the 4.6 palette) | per-node effects inside; the full-screen pass sits on the container (PR-10) | yes (bounded, PR-6 C7) | floors, floor marks, the Y-sorted layer, caps, lights, occluders, fringe, dust, horrors, web, in-world instruments, the camera |
| 1 | **Transit / load hold** | `CanvasLayer` | — | no | no | no | one opaque black quad, shown only in `TRANSIT_HOLD` and `BOOTING/LOADING` (C.2) |
| 2 | **Suit layer (HUD)** | `CanvasLayer` | H | **no** (HR-1 by construction) | no — readings are fed *perceived values* by the Filter as data; the frame is fed nothing (7.6 hand-off) | **never** (HR-13); prompts use the unjolted transform (C11) | critical strip, suit panel, hand rail, crew strip, interaction prompts, inspect card |
| 3 | **Chart table / menus** | `CanvasLayer` | H (bitmap face), continuous (reading face) | no | no | no | pause panel over the frozen world (7.4), web map, settings, text chat |
| 4 | **Debug overlay** | `CanvasLayer`, dev builds only | H | no | **no — it reads the true channel** | no | DIAGNOSTIC surface (C.3); may toggle debug draws *inside* the world viewport (note e) |

Rules that follow: (a) **glow is per viewport** (8.11 flag 3; 4.6 reworked glow to run before tonemapping `[REF]`, so no older tuning transfers and `glow_hdr_threshold` is re-found at 8.12 step 8). (b) The ambient-floor hull material (8.11 flag 1) and the HR-15 low-vision raise are **Lighting's**, applied inside layer 0; the pipeline owns no ambient value and **no full-frame gamma or brightness control exists anywhere** (C-R): the only brightness control the game has is HR-15's bounded hull-material step, which can never reveal web, horrors or filaments and never touches the HUD. (c) In-world instruments are layer-0 lit sprites; the inspect card (7.0) is layer 2 — the same reading drawn twice, once lit and once not. (d) Interaction prompts are layer 2 and are *gated* by the Emitter State exposure query, never by the renderer. (e) Debug draws inside the world (occluder outlines, sort origins, the look-ahead box, the pixel grid, the camera limits) are children of a debug node in layer 0 that exists only in dev builds; `draw_line` there needs explicit width ≥ 1 base px because 4.7 lines have no feather `[REF]`. (f) **NEAREST is set in three places with two differently numbered enums `[BIN]`:** the project setting `rendering/textures/canvas_textures/default_texture_filter = 0` and the world `SubViewport.canvas_item_default_texture_filter = 0` use `Viewport.DEFAULT_CANVAS_ITEM_TEXTURE_FILTER_NEAREST = 0`; the `SubViewportContainer.texture_filter` (a `CanvasItem` member, default `0 = PARENT_NODE`) must be set to `CanvasItem.TEXTURE_FILTER_NEAREST = 1`, or pass A's ×k upscale is bilinear-blurred `[UNV]`. Whether project settings propagate into a `SubViewport` is NOT SOURCEABLE; the startup assertion (PR-15) reads every member back. (g) `SubViewport.size` defaults to 512×512 and `TileSet.tile_size` to 16×16 `[BIN]` — both are set explicitly (640×360 / 48×48); a scene that forgets gets silently wrong output.

*Alternative rejected:* HUD inside the world viewport with `LIGHT_MODE_UNSHADED` materials — unshaded items still receive glow and the full-screen Filter pass, so HR-1 would be a per-node discipline that one forgotten material breaks (8.11 flag 3 made this call; recorded here because the pipeline inherits it).

---

**PR-4. Pixel integrity.** Inside the world viewport:

1. **Nearest sampling everywhere** (`light_` textures excepted — sampled by the light, not the item, 8.4). Mipmaps off on every drawn sheet (8.7).
2. **Integer base-px placement by presentation code — the viewport snap flags are a safety net, not the mechanism** (gameplay-programmer, engine-programmer). Every presentation node computes `pos = floor(prev + (curr − prev) × tick_alpha)` in base px **in the current body frame** and writes that integer; `snap_2d_transforms_to_pixel` and `snap_2d_vertices_to_pixel` are on as belt-and-braces (what they snap to under pass B — base px or render px — is NOT SOURCEABLE; step 12 checks for double-rounding flicker at .5 boundaries). `floor` is the one rounding function used everywhere, including the camera and the beam's chest point (which uses the same rounded position as the sprite, so light origin and sprite never disagree). Because the world canvas *is* the body frame (PR-6 C2), no fractional body offset ever enters an interior position; other bodies drawn in this frame (a docked derelict, a detaching section) are placed by one floored offset shared by all their items, so their items never swim against each other.
3. **Interpolate, then quantise.** Rounding before interpolating produces 1 px stalls; interpolating after rounding is impossible. Consequence to state honestly (engine-programmer): **snap is a floor, not a filter** — interpolation changes only the *timing* of one-base-px steps, never their size. A body moving 1 base px per tick shows a k×k screen block step whenever it moves; the promise is "base-pixel steps at interpolated timing, never twice in a frame at f_render ≥ 60 (below that 1–2 base px per frame at 30–59 fps), never backward", not sub-pixel smoothness *(Amended 2026-10-28 — delegated ruling G4)*. The Player Controller should therefore choose walk and run speeds in **whole base px per tick** when the camera quantum is 1 (PR-6 C3) — routed.
4. **Scale.** Only integer scales, only k (or the zoom step). Horizontal flips are permitted (mirrored facings, 5.6). No per-node scale animation of any kind; `Control.scale` stays `(1,1)` on the HUD. `Camera2D.zoom` stays `(1,1)` **always** (there is no pixel-snap member on `Camera2D` — confirmed by the exhaustive `[BIN]` member list — so zoom is a change of k, PR-6 C6).

# Design Document Rules

- The 8 GDD sections are: Overview, Player Fantasy, Detailed Rules, Formulas, Edge Cases, Dependencies, Tuning Knobs, Acceptance Criteria
- **How many are required depends on `modes.workflow`** — all 8 at `full`, 5 (+ Formulas when the system **defines numeric rules**: rates, curves, thresholds, costs, damage, drop weights — anything a balance pass would tune) at `standard`, none at `minimal` (the design record there is `design/game-brief.md`). Resolve the tier before flagging a section as missing; see `.claude/docs/workflow-modes.md`
- **The Formulas test is what the system defines, not what it is called.** A system's `Category` in `systems-index.md` is a hint — `Gameplay`, `Economy` and `Progression` almost always qualify — never the test. Do not gate Formulas on a category token: the categories `/map-systems` writes (`Core · Gameplay · Progression · Economy · Persistence · UI · Audio · Narrative · Meta`) do not include `combat` or `AI`, which are example systems *within* `Gameplay`. Every site stating this rule must state the same test.
- **Section-name alias**: The GDD template and `/design-system` author this section as `## Detailed Design`; the design standard calls it **Detailed Rules**. These are the SAME required section — accept either heading and never rewrite one into the other.
- Formulas must include variable definitions, expected value ranges, and example calculations
- Edge cases must explicitly state what happens, not just "handle gracefully"
- Dependencies must be bidirectional — if system A depends on B, B's doc must mention A
- Tuning knobs must specify safe ranges and what gameplay aspect they affect
- Acceptance criteria must be testable — a QA tester must be able to verify pass/fail
- No hand-waving: "the system should feel good" is not a valid specification
- Balance values must link to their source formula or rationale
- Design documents MUST be written incrementally: create skeleton first, then fill
  each section one at a time with user approval between sections. Write each
  approved section to the file immediately to persist decisions and manage context

# Design Directory

When authoring or editing files in this directory, follow these standards.

## GDD Files (`design/gdd/`)

The 8 GDD sections, in order:
1. Overview — one-paragraph summary
2. Player Fantasy — intended feeling and experience
3. Detailed Rules — unambiguous mechanics
4. Formulas — all math defined with variables
5. Edge Cases — unusual situations handled
6. Dependencies — other systems listed
7. Tuning Knobs — configurable values identified
8. Acceptance Criteria — testable success conditions

**How many are REQUIRED depends on `modes.workflow`** — all 8 at `full`; 5 at
`standard` (Overview, Detailed Rules, Edge Cases, Dependencies, Acceptance
Criteria, plus Formulas when the system has math); none at `minimal`, where
`design/game-brief.md` is the design record instead of a GDD. Resolve the tier
before flagging a section as missing — see `.claude/docs/workflow-modes.md`.

> **Three other places already encode the tier rule** —
> `.claude/docs/coding-standards.md`, `.claude/rules/design-docs.md` and
> `.claude/hooks/validate-commit.sh`. This file is the copy a session working in
> `design/` reads first, so it must agree with them: demanding all 8 at
> `minimal` warns a jam project about six sections its own configuration says it
> does not need, which trains the user to ignore the warning.

**Section-name alias:** the GDD template and `/design-system` author section 3
as `## Detailed Design`; the standard calls it **Detailed Rules**. Same required
section — accept either heading, never rewrite one into the other.

**File naming:** `[system-slug].md` (e.g. `movement-system.md`, `combat-system.md`)

**Systems index:** `design/gdd/systems-index.md` — update when adding a new GDD.

**Design order:** Foundation → Core → Feature → Presentation → Polish

**Validation:** Run `/design-review [path]` after authoring any GDD.
Run `/review-all-gdds` after completing a set of related GDDs.

## Quick Specs (`design/quick-specs/`)

Lightweight specs for tuning changes, minor mechanics, or balance adjustments.
Use `/quick-design` to author.

## UX Specs (`design/ux/`)

- Per-screen specs: `design/ux/[screen-name].md`
- HUD design: `design/ux/hud.md`
- Interaction pattern library: `design/ux/interaction-patterns.md`
- Accessibility requirements: `design/accessibility-requirements.md`

Use `/ux-design` to author. Validate with `/ux-review` before passing to `/team-ui`.

> **Accessibility requirements sit OUTSIDE `design/ux/` on purpose.** They are a
> project-wide standard the per-screen specs consult, not a spec for one screen.
> `.claude/docs/workflow-catalog.yaml`, the Pre-Production, Production and Polish
> gates, and `/architecture-review` all check `design/accessibility-requirements.md`
> at that exact path. Do not "tidy" it under `design/ux/` — every one of those
> checks would stop matching, and the Technical Setup → Pre-Production gate would
> become unpassable. `/ux-design` states the same rule at its `accessibility` mode.

> `design/` reads first, so it must agree with them: demanding all 8 at
> `minimal` warns a jam project about six sections its own configuration says it
> does not need, which trains the user to ignore the warning.

**Section-name alias:** the GDD template and `/design-system` author section 3
as `## Detailed Design`; the standard calls it **Detailed Rules**. Same required
section — accept either heading, never rewrite one into the other.

**File naming:** `[system-slug].md` (e.g. `movement-system.md`, `combat-system.md`)

**Systems index:** `design/gdd/systems-index.md` — update when adding a new GDD.

**Design order:** Foundation → Core → Feature → Presentation → Polish

**Validation:** Run `/design-review [path]` after authoring any GDD.
Run `/review-all-gdds` after completing a set of related GDDs.

## Quick Specs (`design/quick-specs/`)

Lightweight specs for tuning changes, minor mechanics, or balance adjustments.
Use `/quick-design` to author.

## UX Specs (`design/ux/`)

- Per-screen specs: `design/ux/[screen-name].md`
- HUD design: `design/ux/hud.md`
- Interaction pattern library: `design/ux/interaction-patterns.md`
- Accessibility requirements: `design/accessibility-requirements.md`

Use `/ux-design` to author. Validate with `/ux-review` before passing to `/team-ui`.

> **Accessibility requirements sit OUTSIDE `design/ux/` on purpose.** They are a
> project-wide standard the per-screen specs consult, not a spec for one screen.
> `.claude/docs/workflow-catalog.yaml`, the Pre-Production, Production and Polish
> gates, and `/architecture-review` all check `design/accessibility-requirements.md`
> at that exact path. Do not "tidy" it under `design/ux/` — every one of those
> checks would stop matching, and the Technical Setup → Pre-Production gate would
> become unpassable. `/ux-design` states the same rule at its `accessibility` mode.

# Design Document Rules

- The 8 GDD sections are: Overview, Player Fantasy, Detailed Rules, Formulas, Edge Cases, Dependencies, Tuning Knobs, Acceptance Criteria
- **How many are required depends on `modes.workflow`** — all 8 at `full`, 5 (+ Formulas when the system **defines numeric rules**: rates, curves, thresholds, costs, damage, drop weights — anything a balance pass would tune) at `standard`, none at `minimal` (the design record there is `design/game-brief.md`). Resolve the tier before flagging a section as missing; see `.claude/docs/workflow-modes.md`
- **The Formulas test is what the system defines, not what it is called.** A system's `Category` in `systems-index.md` is a hint — `Gameplay`, `Economy` and `Progression` almost always qualify — never the test. Do not gate Formulas on a category token: the categories `/map-systems` writes (`Core · Gameplay · Progression · Economy · Persistence · UI · Audio · Narrative · Meta`) do not include `combat` or `AI`, which are example systems *within* `Gameplay`. Every site stating this rule must state the same test.
- **Section-name alias**: The GDD template and `/design-system` author this section as `## Detailed Design`; the design standard calls it **Detailed Rules**. These are the SAME required section — accept either heading and never rewrite one into the other.
- Formulas must include variable definitions, expected value ranges, and example calculations
- Edge cases must explicitly state what happens, not just "handle gracefully"
- Dependencies must be bidirectional — if system A depends on B, B's doc must mention A
- Tuning knobs must specify safe ranges and what gameplay aspect they affect
- Acceptance criteria must be testable — a QA tester must be able to verify pass/fail
- No hand-waving: "the system should feel good" is not a valid specification
- Balance values must link to their source formula or rationale
- Design documents MUST be written incrementally: create skeleton first, then fill
  each section one at a time with user approval between sections. Write each
  approved section to the file immediately to persist decisions and manage context

17	
18	## Summary
19	
20	The Pixel-Perfect Render Pipeline & Camera is the surface every visual system draws onto and the window the player sees through: a 640×360 logical world scaled by a whole number to the display, rendered with nearest sampling and pixel snapping so no pixel ever moves without a cause in the world; a HUD on its own layer that world light, the sanity filter and camera motion can never touch; a draw-order contract that makes a 3/4-oblique ship read correctly; and a camera that is a window, not a sensor — it follows the player and leans where their beam points, responds to nothing the world does, holds still when the ship does, and cuts rather than pans. It exists because the art bible's identity (*What You Light, You Can Read*) and three pillars rest on an image that is faithful to the simulation at the scale of one art pixel, and because the lighting-budget spike that decides the renderer's cost cannot run without the pipeline it measures.
21	
22	> **Quick reference** — Layer: `Foundation` · Priority: `MVP` · Key deps: `None` upstream (contracts: Command & Simulation Layer CR-10/11; art bible 8.1–8.4, 7.0); 17 downstream dependents *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*
23	
24	## Overview
25	
26	The Pixel-Perfect Render Pipeline & Camera is the surface every visual system of The Synaptic Sea draws onto, and the window through which the player sees it. It fixes a **logical resolution of 640×360** scaled by an integer to the player's display (3× at 1080p, 4× at 1440p, 6× at 2160p, 2× on a Steam Deck), renders the world into its own viewport with nearest-neighbour sampling and pixel snapping so that every art pixel is a crisp square of screen pixels, keeps the HUD on a separate root-viewport layer that the world's glow, ambient and occlusion can never touch, and owns the **camera**: what it follows, how it moves, where it may not go, and the integer zoom steps it may take. It also owns the draw-order contract that makes a 3/4-oblique ship read correctly — floors never sort, wall faces and actors sort together by Y, caps draw above actors — and the single full-screen hook point where the Perception Filter is allowed to corrupt what a low-sanity player sees, below the HUD and never touching it.
27	
28	The player never interacts with this system directly. They experience it as an image that is faithful: the one-pixel wander of a lying needle and the two-pixel identity bands on a crewmate's helmet stay legible because nothing ever shimmers or blurs; the edge of their own light is drawn as Lighting computes it, never softened or extended by a mask; the frame holds still when the ship does, and moves only as the simulation moves.
29	
30	It exists because the art bible's whole identity rests on it: *What You Light, You Can Read* needs true 2D occlusion (not a vignette), legibility at one art pixel, and a HUD exempt from world light (art bible Principle 1, 7.0, 8.1–8.4), and the lighting-budget spike that decides the renderer's cost (8.12) cannot run without the pipeline it measures. Seventeen systems, across sixteen rows of the Interactions table (Settings & Input Rebinding and Accessibility Settings share one row — see Dependencies), rest on it directly, and every presentation system inherits its contract *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*: subscribe to the kernel as `PRESENTATION`, read last-committed state, interpolate with `tick_alpha`, write only what is drawn (Command & Simulation Layer CR-10, CR-11). Without it, the game would still simulate correctly and look wrong — which, for a game whose pillar is *The World Never Lies*, is the same as being wrong.
31	
32	**Design-level only.** `SubViewport` vs root rendering, stretch and snap settings, whether lights render at base or native resolution (the spike's pass A/B), `Camera2D` smoothing vs manual interpolation — these are implementation choices → **becomes an ADR** (render pipeline / tick-source ADRs). *(Framing: technical infrastructure, no ADR yet to cite, fantasy felt indirectly — the recommended options for a `Core`/`Foundation` system under `autonomous` automation.)*
33	
34	## Player Fantasy
35	
36	*Indirect — the player never meets this system; they meet a stillness it keeps.*
37	
38	**When the ship is still, the screen is still.** The game teaches the player to read motion as evidence. A needle that shakes a pixel is a stressed hull warning them. A needle that glides slowly with nothing in the ship to explain it is lying. The four trim bands on a crewmate's helmet are who that is. All of this lives at the scale of one or two art pixels, so it only works if no pixel ever moves for a reason that isn't in the world: no shimmer from a non-integer scale, no camera crawl from rounding, no actor jittering a pixel against the floor as the camera follows. Every pixel that changes was changed by something in the world.
39	
40	The anchor moment is on the first sortie. The player stands in a dead scrubber bay with their beam on a wall gauge. They stop walking and the frame stops with them. Then the needle moves. Because nothing else on screen moved, the player knows the motion belongs to the ship, or to their own mind, and not to the screen. They lean in to see whether it shakes or glides, and that judgement is the game. The comfort is structural: *if I saw it move, something moved it.*
41	
42	**Pillars served.** *Dread Before Chaos*: "Every breach is preceded by a tell a careful player could have perceived (sound, light, gauge drift, hull stress)" — gauge drift is perceivable only if render noise can neither fake it nor hide it. *Sanity Rewrites Reality*: "the lie extends from the gauge to the sprite" — the art bible's settle/tremor/glide grammar (7.3) is how a player tells the lie from the warning, and a pipeline that adds its own motion corrupts both. *The World Never Lies*: the rendering stack is neither instrument nor perception, so it may not be wrong either. *The Web Watches*: filament movement at ≤ 1 art px/s (art bible 2.11) is readable only on a grid that does not crawl.
43	
44	**Design tests.**
45	- If we are debating a presentation effect that moves world pixels with no cause in the world (sub-pixel smoothing, eased camera lag that overshoots, non-integer zoom, a softening filter, screen shake) against holding the grid: hold the grid, or move the effect into the world (a needle, a sprite, a light).
46	- The fantasy has failed if a player can see a one-art-pixel movement that no system put there. Two cases count: a static scene, and a followed actor that shifts relative to the floor while the camera tracks it. That is a counterfeit tremor or a counterfeit glide — a Pillar 2 and Pillar 4 violation, not a cosmetic bug. It is testable on day one with a frame-diff: hold the sim with no committed change and the camera target still, and the only world pixels allowed to differ between frames are those owned by a declared animating source (flicker, scrolling medium, web drift); then walk an actor across a static room, and the actor-to-floor offset may change only by whole art pixels in step with committed position.
47	
48	*What this section does not claim.* The pipeline does not make the world honest; the kernel does. It does not make motion meaningful; the art bible's grammar does. It does not make a reading true; the HUD frame stays put and undimmed (HR-1), but the needle inside it may lie under class (b). It does not own the edge of the light — Lighting and Principle 1 do; the pipeline's part is only that no mask, vignette, fog layer or edge-darkening ever sits between a lit world pixel and the screen, which is a prohibition in Core Rules, not a fantasy. The image is up to one tick behind committed state and never ahead of it (kernel `tick_alpha` clamps at 1). Under lighting pass A the cone edge is a 3-px stair-step at 1080p, and this section does not promise a smooth one. *(Alternatives considered: "the edge belongs to the light" — evocative but credits the pipeline with Lighting's guarantee; "a porthole, not a lens" — accurate camera policy, but policy is not a moment the player feels.)*
49	
50	**Downstream implications carried into Section C and Game Feel.** Any whole-frame shake counterfeits a tremor, the honest Tell of 2.7: hull stress goes into real needles, dust direction and sprites, not into the frame, and whether any shake survives (e.g. breach impact after the tell has landed) is decided explicitly against design test 1. The commonest way this fantasy fails is the followed actor and the world rounding to different integers in the same frame, so QA tests motion during follow, not only a still scene. The HUD exemption is anchoring, not truth.
51	
52	## Detailed Design
53	
54	### Core Rules
55	
56	*Specialists consulted: systems-designer (primary), engine-programmer, gameplay-programmer, game-designer, ux-designer. Disagreements resolved and logged 2026-10-26; items the specialists could not resolve are in Open Questions.*
57	
58	
59	**Vocabulary.** *Base px* (*art px*): one pixel of the 640×360 logical grid. *Screen px*: one pixel of the window. *k*: the world's integer scale (screen px per base px). *k_base*: the effective base scale — the manual `k` when Settings sets one below Auto, else the automatic `k` (C6, D.5) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. *H*: the HUD's integer scale, independent of k. *Picture*: the region of the window that shows the game (the window unless letterboxed). *World viewport*: the `SubViewport` holding every lit thing; its canvas **is the current body's frame** (PR-6 C2). *Body*: a Ship Body & Interior Physics object with its own reference frame (home-ship, derelict, pod, detached section). *Sort origin*: the base-px row an object sorts by on the Y-sorted layer. *Pose*: the camera's output — integer base-px position in the body frame plus the current k. *`present_time`*: the pipeline's render-rate clock (PR-9). *Tick*, *`tick_alpha`*, *read view*, *`PRESENTATION`*: as the kernel GDD defines them (CR-10, CR-11, D.3).
60	
61	---
62	
63	**PR-1. Logical resolution and integer scale.** The world is authored at **640×360 base px** (registry: `BASE_RESOLUTION`) (art bible 8.1, decided) and drawn at an integer scale `k = floor(min(W / 640, H / 360))` where `W × H` is the window's **pixel** size — never derived from DPI; `content_scale_factor` stays 1.0 and `allow_hidpi` behaviour on the Deck and on Windows ≥ 125 % scaling is logged by spike step 11 (→ D for the variable table). The **minimum window is 1280×720** (registry: `MIN_WINDOW`) (C-R; `Window.min_size` `[BIN]`), so `k ≥ 2` on every display. Nothing in the world is ever drawn at a non-integer scale; the only non-integer text anywhere is the vector reading face on the chart-table layer (7.1). At every window size the player sees square, unblurred base pixels; the trade is the picture size, never pixel integrity. The player may choose k below the automatic value in Settings ("integer world scale: Auto + list", PR-14) — see PR-2 for why a manual k forces `keep`.
64

71	| 1600×900 | 2 | 1280×720, 160/160 L/R, 90/90 T/B (36 % of the screen black) | 800×450 | 16.7 × 9.4 |

73	| 1920×1200 | 3 | 1920×1080, 60/60 T/B | 640×400 | 13.3 × 8.3 |
74	| **2560×1440** | 4 | none | 640×360 | 13.3 × 7.5 |
75	| 2560×1080 (21:9) | 3 | 1920×1080, 320/320 L/R | 852×360 (even; 2/2 residual) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)* | 17.8 × 7.5 |
76	| **3440×1440 (ultrawide)** | 4 | 2560×1440, 440/440 L/R | 860×360 | 17.9 × 7.5 |
77	| **3840×2160** | 6 | none | 640×360 | 13.3 × 7.5 |
78	
79	*Rationale.* 640×360 is the only common base that lands on an integer at 720p, 1080p, 1440p and 2160p (8.1's table), so the four sizes the bible calls common need no policy at all; PR-2 exists for everything else. *Alternative rejected:* fractional scaling with a sharpening filter — it breaks 8.0's single grid and makes the 1 px contour, the 2 px bands and the 2 px fringe uneven widths, which 5.6's minimum-feature rule forbids. *Engine fact that makes this rule load-bearing:* `project.godot` today has no `[display]` block and no `rendering/textures` or `rendering/2d/snap` keys, so the project currently runs at the engine built-ins — 1152×648, stretch `disabled`, `fractional`, LINEAR-filtered, unsnapped `[BIN]` — and looks "almost right" in the editor at 1×. PR-15 is the guard.
80	
81	---
82	
83	**PR-2. Aspect: `keep` for the spike, `expand` as the IDEAL, both bounded; bars are true black.**
84	
85	- **`keep` (letterbox).** The picture is `640k × 360k`, centred; the remainder is bars. This is the spike architecture (8.4) and the **default until 8.12 step 2 and step 11 have run**, because the world viewport is a fixed 640×360 and nothing resizes.
86	- **`expand` (IDEAL, 8.1/8.10, post-spike).** The world viewport's logical size becomes `(2·floor(W/(2k)), 2·floor(H/(2k)))` (always even; D.3), clamped to **≤ 960×540** at default zoom (PROVISIONAL cap = 1.5× base; → D), remainder letterboxed; the base size and k both stay integer at every window (C-R); the **HUD rect is pinned to the `k_base` picture rect** (never the window, never the zoomed picture), so the HUD does not move on a zoom step even when a ladder field leaves a few black pixels inside it (D.5) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. The camera stays centred on the same target, so an ultrawide player sees more void left and right and a Deck player 20 more rows above and below.
87	- **Manual k forces `keep`.** A player-chosen k below the automatic value under `expand` would be a permanently wider frame (at 1080p, k = 2 gives 960×540 — exactly the zoom-out view, as the default), which the game-designer's decision forbids ("never a wider default frame"; the frame is changed only by the player's `zoom_in` / `zoom_out` steps, PR-6 C6 *(Amended 2026-10-26 — consistency check)*). So when `k < k_auto`, aspect is `keep` regardless of the setting. *(Systems-designer resolution of a conflict between the Settings list and the camera decision — flagged for the ux-designer and game-designer to confirm.)*
88	
89	*The honesty caveat on "more void, not more information" (8.1).* The claim holds in the dark states (2.4–2.8), where everything outside the beam is black whichever width the frame is. It does **not** fully hold in two cases: (i) at 3440×1440 under `expand` the half-width is ≈ 9 tiles, so the narrow cone's 8-tile reach (8.3) fits entirely on screen where a 16:9 player's is clipped at 6.7 tiles; (ii) in the home-ship stable state (2.3) every fixture is on and a wider frame shows more lit ship. A 1600×900 player under `expand` sees 25 % more in each axis than a 1080p player. The cap bounds the gap; it does not remove it. **Routed to creative-director** with the recommendation to accept `expand` (a third of the screen black at 1600×900 is a worse experience than a slightly wider frame in a co-op horror game with no competitive stake) and to record the gap in Edge Cases. Second cost: under pass B (PR-7) light is paid per lit screen pixel — 4.95 M px at 3440×1440 against 2.07 M at 1080p; under pass A the cost grows only to 860×360 base px. The spike measures pass B at 1080p only; `expand` under pass B is a post-spike measurement.
90	
91	*Bars.* Letterbox bars are **true black, outside the world `SubViewport`**, untouched by the Perception Filter pass and by any camera jolt (C-R). Because the void inside the world is also near-black (0–1 % ambient, 2.5), a bar could be mistaken for unlit hull: the ux-designer recommends a **1-HUD-px Graphite hairline at the picture edge** — routed to art-director (it is a UI mark, 4.6 palette). What the engine actually draws in the remainder under `keep` is NOT SOURCEABLE (step 11).
92	
93	*Deck safe area (PROVISIONAL).* The HUD is authored **anchor-relative to the visible picture rect**, never the window, with the 7.0 safe margin of 5 % of the picture rounded up to whole HUD px per axis (registry `safe_margin`, the HUD & Suit Layer's formula): 32 × 18 HUD px at 1920×1080, H 3; 22 × 14 HUD px at 1280×800, H 3 *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from hud-and-suit-layer)* — and must survive a fractional HUD canvas (the picture divided by H is not always integer) and both aspects (C-R). The Deck has no notch; the margin is ergonomic and the ux-designer may raise it per device. Deck *text* size is PR-12's problem.
94	
95	*Fullscreen.* Default `MODE_FULLSCREEN` (borderless window covering the screen, `Window.mode = 3` `[BIN]`) rather than `EXCLUSIVE_FULLSCREEN` for Alt-Tab safety `[UNV]`; any mode or size change fires `Viewport.size_changed` `[BIN]` and is handled as one `RESCALING` frame (C.2) by **one pipeline-root node that is the only writer** of `SubViewport.size`, `size_2d_override` and the camera limits rect (consumed by the solver, C8), and the only caller of `HudLayout` (the HUD & Suit Layer's layout function, which computes the HUD anchors) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from hud-and-suit-layer)* (→ ADR, with PR-7's wiring).
96	
97	---
98	
99	**PR-3. The layer model.** One root viewport, one world viewport, and `CanvasLayer`s above it. The question that assigns a thing to a layer is 7.0's: *who produced the information?* — the ship goes in the world and must be lit to read; the suit and the chart table are screen-space and never lit. **The HUD is in a different viewport, not merely a different layer** (engine-programmer): world lights, glow, `CanvasModulate`, the Filter pass on the container and the camera transform cannot reach it by construction, so HR-1, HR-6 and HR-13 are promised structurally. The trade-off is that nothing that must *mix* (a diegetic element lit by the world) may live there — it goes in the world.
100	
101	| # | Layer (bottom → top) | Where | Scaled by | Lit / glow / ambient / occlusion | Perception Filter | Camera jolt | Contents |
102	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
103	| 0 | **World** | `SubViewport` inside a `SubViewportContainer` | k | **yes** — the only layer that is (`use_hdr_2d`, `use_debanding`, filter, snap set on this viewport's own members `[BIN]`; never on the root, which stays SDR-exact for the 4.6 palette) | per-node effects inside; the full-screen pass sits on the container (PR-10) | yes (bounded, PR-6 C7) | floors, floor marks, the Y-sorted layer, caps, lights, occluders, fringe, dust, horrors, web, in-world instruments, the camera |
104	| 1 | **Transit / load hold** | `CanvasLayer` | — | no | no | no | one opaque black quad, shown only in `TRANSIT_HOLD` and `BOOTING/LOADING` (C.2) |
105	| 2 | **Suit layer (HUD)** | `CanvasLayer` | H | **no** (HR-1 by construction) | no — readings are fed *perceived values* by the Filter as data; the frame is fed nothing (7.6 hand-off) | **never** (HR-13); prompts use the unjolted transform (C11) | critical strip, suit panel, hand rail, crew strip, interaction prompts, inspect card |
106	| 3 | **Chart table / menus** | `CanvasLayer` | H (bitmap face), continuous (reading face) | no | no | no | pause panel over the frozen world (7.4), web map, settings, text chat |
107	| 4 | **Debug overlay** | `CanvasLayer`, dev builds only | H | no | **no — it reads the true channel** | no | DIAGNOSTIC surface (C.3); may toggle debug draws *inside* the world viewport (note e) |
108	
109	Rules that follow: (a) **glow is per viewport** (8.11 flag 3; 4.6 reworked glow to run before tonemapping `[REF]`, so no older tuning transfers and `glow_hdr_threshold` is re-found at 8.12 step 8). (b) The ambient-floor hull material (8.11 flag 1) and the HR-15 low-vision raise are **Lighting's**, applied inside layer 0; the pipeline owns no ambient value and **no full-frame gamma or brightness control exists anywhere** (C-R): the only brightness control the game has is HR-15's bounded hull-material step, which can never reveal web, horrors or filaments and never touches the HUD. (c) In-world instruments are layer-0 lit sprites; the inspect card (7.0) is layer 2 — the same reading drawn twice, once lit and once not. (d) Interaction prompts are layer 2 and are *gated* by the Emitter State exposure query, never by the renderer. (e) Debug draws inside the world (occluder outlines, sort origins, the look-ahead box, the pixel grid, the camera limits) are children of a debug node in layer 0 that exists only in dev builds; `draw_line` there needs explicit width ≥ 1 base px because 4.7 lines have no feather `[REF]`. (f) **NEAREST is set in three places with two differently numbered enums `[BIN]`:** the project setting `rendering/textures/canvas_textures/default_texture_filter = 0` and the world `SubViewport.canvas_item_default_texture_filter = 0` use `Viewport.DEFAULT_CANVAS_ITEM_TEXTURE_FILTER_NEAREST = 0`; the `SubViewportContainer.texture_filter` (a `CanvasItem` member, default `0 = PARENT_NODE`) must be set to `CanvasItem.TEXTURE_FILTER_NEAREST = 1`, or pass A's ×k upscale is bilinear-blurred `[UNV]`. Whether project settings propagate into a `SubViewport` is NOT SOURCEABLE; the startup assertion (PR-15) reads every member back. (g) `SubViewport.size` defaults to 512×512 and `TileSet.tile_size` to 16×16 `[BIN]` — both are set explicitly (640×360 / 48×48); a scene that forgets gets silently wrong output.
110	
111	*Alternative rejected:* HUD inside the world viewport with `LIGHT_MODE_UNSHADED` materials — unshaded items still receive glow and the full-screen Filter pass, so HR-1 would be a per-node discipline that one forgotten material breaks (8.11 flag 3 made this call; recorded here because the pipeline inherits it).
112	
113	---
114	
115	**PR-4. Pixel integrity.** Inside the world viewport:
116	
117	1. **Nearest sampling everywhere** (`light_` textures excepted — sampled by the light, not the item, 8.4). Mipmaps off on every drawn sheet (8.7).
118	2. **Integer base-px placement by presentation code — the viewport snap flags are a safety net, not the mechanism** (gameplay-programmer, engine-programmer). Every presentation node computes `pos = floor(prev + (curr − prev) × tick_alpha)` in base px **in the current body frame** and writes that integer; `snap_2d_transforms_to_pixel` and `snap_2d_vertices_to_pixel` are on as belt-and-braces (what they snap to under pass B — base px or render px — is NOT SOURCEABLE; step 12 checks for double-rounding flicker at .5 boundaries). `floor` is the one rounding function used everywhere, including the camera and the beam's chest point (which uses the same rounded position as the sprite, so light origin and sprite never disagree). Because the world canvas *is* the body frame (PR-6 C2), no fractional body offset ever enters an interior position; other bodies drawn in this frame (a docked derelict, a detaching section) are placed by one floored offset shared by all their items, so their items never swim against each other.
119	3. **Interpolate, then quantise.** Rounding before interpolating produces 1 px stalls; interpolating after rounding is impossible. Consequence to state honestly (engine-programmer): **snap is a floor, not a filter** — interpolation changes only the *timing* of one-base-px steps, never their size. A body moving 1 base px per tick shows a k×k screen block step whenever it moves; the promise is "base-pixel steps at interpolated timing, never twice in a frame at f_render ≥ 60 (below that 1–2 base px per frame at 30–59 fps), never backward", not sub-pixel smoothness *(Amended 2026-10-28 — delegated ruling G4)*. The Player Controller should therefore choose walk and run speeds in **whole base px per tick** when the camera quantum is 1 (PR-6 C3) — routed.
120	4. **Scale.** Only integer scales, only k (or the zoom step). Horizontal flips are permitted (mirrored facings, 5.6). No per-node scale animation of any kind; `Control.scale` stays `(1,1)` on the HUD. `Camera2D.zoom` stays `(1,1)` **always** (there is no pixel-snap member on `Camera2D` — confirmed by the exhaustive `[BIN]` member list — so zoom is a change of k, PR-6 C6).

# Design Document Rules

- The 8 GDD sections are: Overview, Player Fantasy, Detailed Rules, Formulas, Edge Cases, Dependencies, Tuning Knobs, Acceptance Criteria

# Design Directory

When authoring or editing files in this directory, follow these standards.

## GDD Files (`design/gdd/`)

The 8 GDD sections, in order:
1. Overview — one-paragraph summary
2. Player Fantasy — intended feeling and experience
3. Detailed Rules — unambiguous mechanics
4. Formulas — all math defined with variables
5. Edge Cases — unusual situations handled
6. Dependencies — other systems listed
7. Tuning Knobs — configurable values identified
8. Acceptance Criteria — testable success conditions

**How many are REQUIRED depends on `modes.workflow`** — all 8 at `full`; 5 at
`standard` (Overview, Detailed Rules, Edge Cases, Dependencies, Acceptance
Criteria, plus Formulas when the system has math); none at `minimal`, where
`design/game-brief.md` is the design record instead of a GDD. Resolve the tier
before flagging a section as missing — see `.claude/docs/workflow-modes.md`.

> **Three other places already encode the tier rule** —
> `.claude/docs/coding-standards.md`, `.claude/rules/design-docs.md` and
> `.claude/hooks/validate-commit.sh`. This file is the copy a session working in
> `design/` reads first, so it must agree with them: demanding all 8 at
> `minimal` warns a jam project about six sections its own configuration says it
> does not need, which trains the user to ignore the warning.

**Section-name alias:** the GDD template and `/design-system` author section 3
as `## Detailed Design`; the standard calls it **Detailed Rules**. Same required
section — accept either heading, never rewrite one into the other.

**File naming:** `[system-slug].md` (e.g. `movement-system.md`, `combat-system.md`)

**Systems index:** `design/gdd/systems-index.md` — update when adding a new GDD.

**Design order:** Foundation → Core → Feature → Presentation → Polish

**Validation:** Run `/design-review [path]` after authoring any GDD.
Run `/review-all-gdds` after completing a set of related GDDs.

## Quick Specs (`design/quick-specs/`)

Lightweight specs for tuning changes, minor mechanics, or balance adjustments.
Use `/quick-design` to author.

## UX Specs (`design/ux/`)

- Per-screen specs: `design/ux/[screen-name].md`
- HUD design: `design/ux/hud.md`
- Interaction pattern library: `design/ux/interaction-patterns.md`
- Accessibility requirements: `design/accessibility-requirements.md`

Use `/ux-design` to author. Validate with `/ux-review` before passing to `/team-ui`.

> **Accessibility requirements sit OUTSIDE `design/ux/` on purpose.** They are a
> project-wide standard the per-screen specs consult, not a spec for one screen.
> `.claude/docs/workflow-catalog.yaml`, the Pre-Production, Production and Polish
> gates, and `/architecture-review` all check `design/accessibility-requirements.md`
> at that exact path. Do not "tidy" it under `design/ux/` — every one of those
> checks would stop matching, and the Technical Setup → Pre-Production gate would
> become unpassable. `/ux-design` states the same rule at its `accessibility` mode.

</system-reminder>

`37.4 + 72 = 109.4 > 108` by 1.4 px, so the inner box engages (`diag.inner_box_engaged`, a 1.4 px pin) in that regime and the build asserts the worst case `n_max·v_max/60·(1 − a)/a < LAG_CUT` (37.4 < 48, no cut) rather than `< INNER_BOX_FRAC·field_h − L_MAX_eff` (accepted engagement, documented, never a cut); rewritten 2026-10-27 — design review for world-anchored bands)*; `H_default ≥ 3`; `k_min = 2`; `Q ∈ {1, 1/k}`; `JOLT_MAX ≤ 2`; `F_MAX = 3`; `SETTLE_EPS ≤ 0.5·Q`; `LEAN_R1 > LEAN_R0 ≥ 8` (PC-5's mouse dead-zone, base px) *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. *(Amended 2026-10-26 — consistency check.)*
944	
945	## Visual/Audio Requirements
946	
947	The pipeline draws nothing of its own and plays nothing. What it *requires* of visual systems is the contract in Section C: every presentation element lives in the world `SubViewport` or on the root HUD layer, never both; every sprite and tile is placed at integer base pixels by presentation code (the viewport snap flags are a safety net, not the mechanism); human-built geometry never rotates at runtime; horror rigs and web pieces rotate only in the quantised steps the art bible fixes; VFX and one-off sprites use even cell sizes or `centered = false` with an integer offset so no origin lands on a half pixel; hairlines are sprites, never 1-px line draws (4.7 draws lines without an antialiasing feather). Two art-bible rules become pipeline rules here: the only brightness control in the game is the bounded ambient-floor step implemented as the hull-material raise (HR-15; no full-frame gamma or brightness exists), and letterbox bars, where they occur, are true black outside the world and get a 1-HUD-px Graphite hairline at the viewport edge so a bar is never read as unlit hull (routed to art-director); the hairline is a layer-1 element, excluded from the HUD's critical-strip count *(Amended 2026-10-27 — consistency pass, routed from hud-and-suit-layer)*. The art bible's 8.2 projection wording carries the Y-sortable convention (height projects up-screen; faces occlude screen-north) since the 2026-10-26 amendment; the spike's Y-sort room remains its test *(Amended 2026-10-27 — design review)*. Audio: none, except that the pipeline's render-rate loop is not the sim clock and audio cues keyed to tells must come from the simulation's notifications, never from frame events. No asset-spec flag: there are no assets.

The pipeline draws nothing of its own and plays nothing. What it *requires* of visual systems is the contract in Section C: every presentation element lives in the world `SubViewport` or on the root HUD layer, never both; every sprite and tile is placed at integer base pixels by presentation code (the viewport snap flags are a safety net, not the mechanism); human-built geometry never rotates at runtime; horror rigs and web pieces rotate only in the quantised steps the art bible fixes; VFX and one-off sprites use even cell sizes or `centered = false` with an integer offset so no origin lands on a half pixel; hairlines are sprites, never 1-px line draws (4.7 draws lines without an antialiasing feather). Audio: none, except that the pipeline's render-rate loop is not the sim clock and audio cues keyed to tells must come from the simulation's notifications, never from frame events.
